"To crow" means to make a loud, triumphant sound — the kind that announces something good has happened. Whether it's an animal, a baby, or a person, crowing is always about expressing victory, joy, or pride out loud and boldly.

In its most basic sense, "to crow" is what a rooster does when it makes its loud, sharp, piercing call — most famously at dawn.

"The rooster crowed before the sun had even risen."

This is where all other meanings grow from. The rooster doesn't just make a sound — it announces itself to the world. That feeling of bold, loud announcement carries into every other use of the word.

This is the meaning you will encounter most in everyday English. When a person crows, they boast loudly and enthusiastically about something they're proud of — a success, a win, an achievement. But "crow" isn't just a neutral word for boasting. It carries a clear emotional color: the person doing it comes across as self-satisfied, a little obnoxious, and repetitive. They're not just happy — they're making sure everyone knows it, loudly and repeatedly.

"He crowed about his salary raise for the entire week."
"She crowed about winning the debate tournament to anyone who would listen."

Imagine someone walking around with their chest puffed out, loudly repeating their success over and over. That's crowing.

Does "crow" always make the person sound bad?

Mostly yes, but not always. The word usually signals that the speaker finds the boasting excessive or irritating. But occasionally, it's used neutrally or even with admiration — especially when the person has genuinely earned the right to boast.

"After ten years of struggle, he had every right to crow."

In this case, the speaker is almost giving permission to boast. But in the majority of everyday contexts, "crow" signals: too much, too loud, too self-congratulatory.
Meaning 3: A Baby's Happy Sounds (Less Common)

"Crow" can also describe the joyful, excited little sounds a baby makes when it's very happy — something like an enthusiastic gurgle or squeal of delight.

"The baby crowed happily when she saw her father walk in."

This use is entirely warm and positive — no negative connotation at all. The connection to the other meanings is the sound itself: babies crowing sound like tiny, triumphant noises of pure joy.

"Crow" in the boasting sense is almost always intransitive — it doesn't need a direct object. Instead, it's typically followed by a preposition:

crow about something → boasting about an achievement or possession:
"She crowed about getting the top marks in class."

crow over someone → gloating over a person, particularly after defeating them or seeing them fail:
"The team crowed over their rivals' poor performance."

You can also use it without any following phrase when the context is already clear:
"He won, and he crowed."

• crow / crows — present tense (She crows about it constantly.)
  • crowing — present participle (He is crowing about his new house.)
  • crowed — past tense and past participle (She crowed about her win for days.)

A small note: In very old or literary writing, you might occasionally see "crew" as the past tense — specifically for the rooster sense ("the cock crew"). But this is archaic. In all modern English, for all meanings, crowed is the correct past tense.

It really helps to see where "crow" fits among nearby words:

Boast / Brag — These simply mean to speak too proudly about yourself. They're relatively neutral in tone. "Crow" goes further — it adds the sense of a loud, almost animal-like triumphant noise. It feels more visceral, more excessive.

Gloat — To gloat is to take quiet, private pleasure in someone else's misfortune or your own win. It's internal and silent, often with a smug little smile. Crowing is the complete opposite: it's external, loud, and directed at others.

Exult — To feel and express great joy and triumph. "Exult" sounds dignified and noble, like a general who has won a long war. "Crow" sounds noisy and slightly rough — like someone who just can't contain themselves.

A useful mental image: Gloating is a quiet, satisfied smirk. Crowing is jumping up and shouting about it.

A very common expression in English is to tell someone "don't crow too soon" — meaning, don't celebrate your victory before it's actually confirmed. It connects directly to the rooster, which sometimes crows at the very first hint of light before full dawn has arrived — announcing something prematurely.

"He started crowing about the win before the final results were even in."

This is a natural, frequently used phrase you'll hear in sports, politics, business, and everyday conversation.

1. "The politician couldn't resist crowing over the opposition's defeat."
  2. "Even her closest friends got tired of her crowing about her new car."
  3. "The startup crowed about its latest funding round on every social media platform."
  4. "I know you did well on the exam, but please stop crowing — others didn't do as well."
  5. "The child crowed with delight when he tore open his birthday present." (joyful sounds, not boasting)
  6. "She scored the winning goal and crowed, but her teammates didn't mind — she'd earned it."

To crow means:

  • (Of a rooster) to make its characteristic loud call.
  • (Of a person) to boast loudly and triumphantly, in a way that tends to come across as excessive and self-satisfied — usually used with about or over.
  • (Of a baby) to make excited, happy sounds of delight.

The emotional core across all three meanings is the same: a loud, uninhibited announcement of joy or triumph. In people, that quality tips over into something a little too much — which is why the word almost always carries at least a gentle note of criticism.
